body.heading: The last five minutes set the tone
paragraphs: However the day went, the last few minutes before sleep are the ones that echo. A small, predictable goodnight ritual — same words, same order — gives a child a safe full stop to the day and a gentle bridge into sleep.
It does not need to be elaborate. A drink of water, one page or one song, the words, the light. Short and identical beats long and improvised.

body.heading: Words worth borrowing
paragraphs: Families invent their own lines, and the invented ones are the best. Common shapes: a list of the people who love them, a thank-you for one thing from the day, a wish for tomorrow, or a call-and-response — 'I love you' / 'I love you more' — that neither side is allowed to win.
A grumpy day can be included honestly: 'today was hard, and I still love you, and tomorrow is a new one.' Children do not need the day rewritten; they need it closed kindly.

body.heading: Keep it when they grow
paragraphs: The words can travel: said at the door of a teenager's room, sent in a message on a school trip, whispered to a baby who cannot understand them yet. Rituals that survive growing up are the ones nobody was forced to keep.
If a child outgrows the words and finds them embarrassing, let them shrink to a knock, a wave, a single word. The shape can change; the closing of the day together is what matters.

description: A few predictable words at the end of the day give children a safe full stop — and they tend to stay in the family for years.
